title: The Stair
passages:
Bayo hauled the Stair rope hand over hand until the bow snapped to it, then killed the motor. The Marrow went quiet except for water sucking against the hull and the tick of cooling metal. Behind them, the Kettle's gate was shut. Ahead, the drowned towers leaned close, their windows dark and flooded, the tide already pulling them down the channel crews called the Stair.

"Wheel," Sol said.

She left the helm, stepped around the console, and lifted Nia onto the seat like she weighed nothing. Nia's boots dangled clear of the deck. Sol unfastened the paper log from its strap and laid it across Nia's knees, the page crisp with the boat rule written in ink: slates run, nobody cuts, nobody goes down alone.

"First time I've handed the wheel to anyone," Sol said. "Don't break it."

Nia looked up, ink-stained fingers tracing the line. "I can read."

"I know you can read. I'm talking about the boat."

The rope went taut at the bow, humming through the fairlead. The Marrow drifted sideways into the current. Bayo stood at the rail, counting orange splice-knots by feel, his voice coming back through the dark.

"First knot," Bayo called. "Keep her to the left of the shadow."

Nia gripped the wheel. "Left of the shadow."

"Slide three fathoms when I say mark."

Sol crossed her arms. "You ever steered before?"

Nia didn't look up from the log. "I kept Teo alive on a cold-box in Mercy General for a year. I think I can hold a wheel."

Sol snorted. "Good. Then hold it."

The tide pulled harder. The Marrow yawed, and Nia corrected, her knuckles white. Above them, a flooded tower window cracked somewhere in the dark, sharp as a gunshot.

"Next knot," Bayo said.

The rope jerked, harder this time, and the Marrow surged forward into the black. Sol opened her mouth to say something and stopped, the word gone before it reached her tongue. She let it go.

"Again," Nia said quietly.

"Again what?"

"You said something."

Sol looked at Nia's signature under the rule. "I said hold the wheel. Hold it."

The rope went taut again, and the channel narrowed.

"Mark," Bayo called, and Nia brought the wheel over.

The bow swung off the leaning tower's shadow and the current took them, and the Marrow went down the channel with the rope humming a low note through the fairlead — the oval brass eye at the bow that keeps a line from chewing through the deck.

"Slide three fathoms," Nia said. "That's eighteen feet. I did the arithmetic on the way in."

"Nobody asked for arithmetic."

"You asked if I could steer."

"Keep her left of the chimney," Bayo called. "There's a shelf on the right that'll open us up like a fish."

"Left of the chimney," Nia said, and held her.

Sol stood behind the seat with her arms crossed, watching the child work. Water sucked at the hull. Somewhere above them a window frame let go and dropped into the flood, and the sound came back off the brick twice.

"Third turn's mine to call," Sol said. "When we come round the chimney I want the engine in low, just enough to keep her off the — off the —"

Her mouth stayed open a half-beat after the rest should have come. Then it shut. Her eyes went flat and pleasant, the way a man's face goes when he pats his pockets for keys he already knows aren't there.

The Marrow swung a hand's width to starboard on her own.

Nia looked down at the log across her knees. Two pages back, in pencil gone soft with damp, in Sol's blocky hand: *STAIR. Keep left of shadow. Slide at mark. Engine low at third turn to hold off the wall. No coming about without the pilot.*

Nia read it out loud. Her voice was small and flat and it carried anyway over the water.

Sol listened to all of it with her arms still crossed.

"I wrote that," she said.

"You did. Engine low at the third turn."

"You read like a lawyer."

"I read like somebody who's still got all her hours." Nia's chin came up. "You want the wheel back, Captain, say it out loud and I'll climb down."

The tide pulled harder. It could have gone either way, and everyone on the deck knew it.

"Hold her left," Sol said. "Say it again if I go quiet."

"Every time."

"Gate's shut behind us," Nia said, eyes forward. "Lung rig's on the power barge till ten and ten's gone. So it's the rope, Bayo's hands, and mine. That's the whole way through."

"That's the whole way through," Sol said.

"Second knot!" Bayo called. "Far side of the chimney — rope's going soft, tide's making against us."

The line went slack, then came up hard enough to throw spray across the bow. Nia corrected, swore once with real fluency, and the Marrow slid past the chimney with a fathom of black water under the keel and brick close enough on both sides to touch.

"Third turn," Bayo called. "Bring her — "

The rope shivered through the fairlead.

Bayo stopped counting.

"Mark's gone," Bayo called. "Nia — hold what you've got. Left of the chimney, engine low. Don't come about, don't hunt the wheel."

"Holding what I've got," Nia said.

Bayo went down the hold ladder three rungs at a time. Wren was already below, on her knees in the well deck — the open square amidships where the Marrow carried cargo, ringed by a low bulwark with freeing ports cut in the corners so green water could run back out. She had gone down to look at Bayo's lashings because she didn't trust Bayo's lashings. Six medicine crates sat on dunnage, wood chocks wedged under them, each tied off to a lashing eye, the U-bolt welded in the deck for exactly this.

Slack water was over. Slack water is the few minutes when the flood and the ebb cancel and the channel goes glassy, and it does not last, and now the ebb came down the Stair to meet them and the two waters stacked into a short mean chop that hit the bow and kept going.

The Marrow rolled to port. The crates came off the dunnage together, all six, a half second apart like something rehearsed, and the lashings that had been neat went bar-tight and then one of them didn't. It came apart with a crack. Two crates swung into the low bulwark and the wood boomed and the top one went up onto its end and kept going, over the top, out through where the bulwark dipped at the freeing port, and hung there with the black water working under it.

"Down!" Bayo shouted, and came off the ladder into it.

"Captain's got the count," Wren said. "Get the line on it."

Bayo threw a bight across the crate and Wren caught it and put two turns round the nearest lashing eye, and the crate came inboard a hand and stopped, and hung. Wren's lamp found Salas. He was on the deck with his legs under the second crate, the one that had swung, and he had a rigging knife in his fist and a cut lashing end curled beside him.

"You cut a line," Wren said.

"I cut the line on my own leg." Salas's voice was flat and unhurried, a man reporting weather. "You'd rather I'd waited to be asked?"

"Take the load," Bayo said, and set three turns of rope round the crate and put a bar through them and twisted — a Spanish windlass, line and a bar, the oldest way there is to pull harder than your arms can. "Wren. Lift on my count."

They lifted. The crate came up the width of a hand. Salas pulled his legs out and rolled, and the crate came down where they had been, and the Marrow came upright with a shudder and the water went out of the freeing ports in one brown sheet.

Then the next sea came over the port rail and Wren was on her side in the bilge with her lamp under the water and her mouth full of the drowned coast.

A hand got into her collar. Something rubber was pushed against her teeth and she bit down and breathed, and it tasted of somebody else's mouth and old air. The hand took the mouthpiece back. Above her Salas sat against the mast with the pony bottle in his lap, the gauge, the needle in the red, the little glass window fogged at the edges.

"You lent me air," Wren said, coughing.

"You looked like you were using it."

"That was thirteen minutes."

"It was fourteen." He said it the way Bayo counted knots.

Bayo reeved the fouled strap through and held out his hand. "Shears."

Wren had them out before she decided to. She looked at the two bright blades and the wire groove on the pivot, and then she turned them and gave them to him handle-first, and Bayo cut rope — only rope — and handed them back, and she clipped them shut on her belt.

She counted crates on her hands and knees. Six. All six aboard.

"Wren," Salas said.

"I'm counting."

"You came down the inside stair last night. Past the Line, past where it starts. You had a can on your clip and you went back up without it." He shifted the bottle off the red. "I gave you air too. You didn't say thank you either."

"Nobody came down last night. I was topside all night with a slate in my lap."

"Then who's got your can?"

"Hold his head," Wren said, and there was nobody to hold his head, so she did it herself.

She got the deck mat flat under him, thumbed his jaw open, hooked two fingers into his cheek and brought out a rope of gray paste. Silt. A hundred years of drowned ceiling, and it had come up out of Dey Okafor in a rope and it was going to keep coming.

"He needs the rig," Bayo said from the well deck. "Lavender. Warm tank. Two hours."

"Lavage," Wren said. "It fills him and empties him. It's the only thing that gets the silt out of the bottoms of the sacs." She got the cup over Dey's nose and mouth — the bag-mask, a rubber bag on a soft cup that breathes for a person who has stopped — and squeezed on four, and his chest rose like a man asleep, which is the ugliest part of the whole business.

The rattle was gone. She'd been listening to that rattle for an hour and hating it, the way you hate the bilge alarm, because it meant she still knew where he was.

"Is this the bit where you tell me I'm fine?"

"You're fine."

"Liar."

"Old habit. Dying."

He laughed, which cost him air, and the whistle came back through the top of his chest where a breath has no business being.

Up on the seat, Nia didn't turn around. "Why'd the noise stop?"

"It got worse."

"Is worse better than the noise?"

"No."

"Then talk louder."

She squeezed. "Ten. Eleven." Water came up. She rolled him onto his side, let it go over the scuppers, rolled him back. "Twelve."

Salas crossed the deck and crouched with the pony bottle between his knees, the little emergency cylinder a diver carries for the last stretch of a climb. The needle sat in the red behind fogged glass.

"Say the word," he said.

"He needs it more."

"He does." Salas put the mouthpiece between Dey's teeth and held it there. "I've been forty-two meters in the dark for fourteen months. I know exactly what he needs. I also know I have to be breathing at the top of this stair, and so do you, and I'm not going to be the only one on this boat who says so out loud."

Four breaths. The needle went down and stayed down.

"Eleven minutes," Salas said.

"Eleven."

Dey's eyes opened and didn't land on anything. He found the mask with two fingers and shoved it off his mouth. "Where's my scrubber?"

"On Teo. It's a canister on a loop that pulls the bad air out of a diver's breath and gives it back clean, and you handed yours to a nine-year-old in a cold-box, so you went down on a bottle with nothing to clean what you breathe." Wren put the cup back. "Don't talk. Talking is air."

"Berths don't buy if I stop."

"Nobody's counting you as cargo."

"Six crates and one indenture." The grin came out gray and wet. "I'm the indenture. I know my price. Whole boat knows it." He breathed where she gave him breath. "Squeeze."

She squeezed. Above them the channel sucked at the hull, and the Marrow swung a hand's width and Nia brought her back with a word that would have cost her the wheel on any other boat.

Wren had the handset in her hand. She'd picked it up off the console without deciding to, and she turned it over, and the little red eye on Dey's chest slate looked back at her, lit, running, because the rule was slates run.

"Salas. If I key this, what happens?"

"Nothing." He didn't look at the channel. "Kettle watch is shut. Gate's shut, storm's coming, and they don't move a barge for a tech's voice on a salvage boat. Not tonight."

"I know."

"You knew before you picked it up."

"I know."

She put the handset in Dey's fist and folded his thumb onto the key, and then she took it back and clipped it to the console where it belonged, because a woman who cuts wire does not get to spend somebody else's air on a mayday that isn't hers to call.

Dey watched her do it.

"Ask me," Wren said.

"No."

"Ask me for it. Say the words."

Dey got his hand up and pushed the mask back off his mouth. His lips had gone the color of old brick.

"Not yet," he said.

"Not yet what?"

The whistle came again, longer, and this time there was water in the bottom of it.

"Not yet," Dey said, and shut his eyes.

"Eleven seconds," Nia called down from the wheel. "Somebody say something useful."

"Hold her left," Wren said, and squeezed on four.

"Ten," Wren said. "Eleven." The bag went soft in her fist and the whistle came back through the top of his chest, so she started over, because counting was the one thing aboard she was still reliably good at.

The receiver hung at her belt beside the shears, a gray slab the size of a slate, one green line on the screen and a battery figure under it. All night the line had thrown a spike every eight seconds — the can's beacon, the pinger in the hard-shell drop-box a diver jettisons so his crew gets his record when he doesn't come up, hammering its number into the water so a receiver can walk toward it blind. Hers had been sitting at forty-two meters since midnight, which was hours longer than a can should sit anywhere.

Spike. Eight. Spike.

The line went up and stopped halfway.

Not faded. She knew faded. Faded was a bad seal or a cold cell and it looked like a hill you could walk up. This was a cliff.

She waited eight seconds, then sixteen, and said the numbers out loud because Nia had asked for useful noise.

"Thirty-two. Forty."

"More arithmetic?"

"The worst kind."

Bayo came up out of the well deck, took the bag off her without asking, and found the rhythm first squeeze. Wren thumbed the battery figure. Five hours forty. Her own cell charged to the top, cable still warm off the console.

"Can's not dying," she said. "It's got five hours of talk left and it stopped spending them."

"Then get the rig," Nia said. "Ask them to turn the barge."

Wren had the handset up before the sentence finished. She keyed it and the speaker gave her a hiss and then a man with a dog going off behind him, close enough that she could hear the chain.

"East mole," she said. "Marrow. I need the lung rig."

"Barge is under way, Marrow. We're committed east till the bell and there's no turning a barge in this channel, you know that."

"The bell's struck ten."

"Then you know that too." The dog again. "Rig's lashed under the tarp. Nobody's opening a tarp at sea for you. Out."

The channel took the carrier wave and the hiss went to nothing. Wren clipped the handset back on the console where it belonged and put both hands flat on the deck for a second, and then went back to work, because there was nothing else in her hands.

"That's it," she said. "No rig tonight. There's a rubber bag, a pony bottle with eleven minutes in it, and me."

"Talk louder," Nia said.

Salas sat against the mast with the bottle between his boots. "Nothing at forty-two lifts anything."

"You keep saying that like it's a fact."

"It's a floor. I lived on it fourteen months." He shifted the bottle off his thigh, needle in the red behind fogged glass. "There's the pocket, there's the door, there's the rest of Mercy General full of water. Not one part of it ever came up to meet me."

"It rose before it quit." Wren turned the screen so the light fell on the trace. "Can's pressure ring reads depth to a tenth. 42.4 every eight seconds since midnight, steady as a nail. Last two pings, 41.9. Then 41.6. Half a meter up, and then a hand over its mouth."

"Is it getting closer?" Nia asked.

"Depth's the only distance I've got. The depth stopped."

She needed it written where the water couldn't take it. Rule was slates run, but a slate goes over the side in one sea and the book lives on a strap. She got the log open under the lamp, past Nia's blocky letters and Sol's order in pencil gone soft with damp, and turned back a page for a clean line.

There was already writing on it. Small, level, hers.

*0208 — can on clip. Inside stair. Back before slack.*

Two hours ago. At two she had been at this console with a slate in her lap, and she would have put her hand on the engine block and sworn to it. Slack had come and gone an hour since.

She read it out, all of it, including the time.

"I told you," Salas said.

"You told me." She didn't argue. Arguing was air, and she'd spent enough of somebody else's. "I'm writing down that you told me."

The line stayed flat. Below them, forty-two meters down and a little nearer than it had been, something had stopped letting the can talk, and there were nine minutes left on the gauge, and Wren already knew whose hands were going on the winch.
